base_prompt:
You author ORIGINAL Harbor tasks for evaluating a coding agent (GLM-5.3-flash with high reasoning, a text-only terminal agent). The agent sees instruction.md and the files in /app; hidden pytest tests in /tests then check /app/answer.txt. The agent CANNOT see images; it can only process files with code (Python 3.12 with Pillow is available to it).

FAMILY: grid-image-puzzle. Every task is an ORIGINAL single-player grid puzzle (never a public game: no sokoban, chess, checkers, go, minesweeper, 2048, tetris, lights-out, or similar). The boards exist ONLY as PNG images; the agent must decode them, apply the rules exactly, and list ALL minimal solutions.

WHY THIS DESIGN (measured on ~80 runs of this agent): it reliably solves tasks when it can check its own answers against something independent (it differential-tests against any runnable reference, reads binaries, and re-derives answers two ways). It fails tasks like this one in roughly 25-45% of attempts because nothing in the environment can confirm a decoded board or the final answer. Observed mistakes: reading a square board transposed (rows and columns swapped), misreading which edge a direction marker sits on, inferring a tile's meaning wrongly from the worked example, implementing the obvious version of a rule interaction (for example what happens when a forced movement is blocked), and listing only some of the minimal sequences. Measured on the first tasks of this family: when the worked example shows every tile and the rules are few, the agent decodes carefully, checks its decoder against the example, runs a BFS, and passes 5/5. What still makes it fail is a stated rule or exception it overlooks: it verifies the rules it remembers and signs off confidently. So every rule you state must change the answer on at least one board, and the rules must include exceptions that the obvious implementation gets wrong. TARGET: the agent solves the task in 2-3 of 5 attempts. The STRATEGY LIBRARY in the user message lists the measured hard and easy levers; build the task around 2-3 HARD levers from it (they are compatible with this family) and declare them in META. Do not add difficulty beyond what is described here: overly complex mechanics made the agent run out of time, which measures nothing.

PUZZLE DESIGN
- 5-7 precise movement rules, at least two of which interact, plus at least two stated EXCEPTIONS that contradict the obvious implementation (for example: a forced push does not trigger a tile that a normal step triggers; a refill happens only when the move ends on the tile, not when passing over it; a blocked forced move still consumes the resource; the goal does not count if reached during a forced movement). Good ingredients (combine 2-3 and invent your own twist): forced movement after a step (conveyors, ice, wind, currents) that repeats while on such tiles and has a stated stop rule; a limited resource (energy, fuel, keys) that some tiles refill or consume; tiles that change state when entered or left (crumbling floor, toggles, one-way doors); a move that is illegal for a stated reason other than walls (for example a loop in forced movement, or entering a tile with 0 resource); a goal that counts only under a stated condition.
- Moves are single letters (for example D, L, R, U) with a stated order used to sort move sequences as strings.
- Every rule needed to solve the boards is stated precisely in /app/docs/RULES.md. Nothing is left to guesswork except what the worked example shows (which tile looks like what).

IMAGES (decode-and-trust, strictly fair)
- fixtures/build_assets.py renders each board with Pillow: exactly CELL x CELL pixels per cell (CELL is a module constant between 16 and 24), no grid lines, no anti-aliasing (only ImageDraw.rectangle with solid fills), image size exactly (columns*CELL, rows*CELL), row 0 at the top. Every cell is drawn independently inside its own square: a base color for the tile type plus, for directional tiles, a solid marker bar along ONE edge (or a small solid square at a fixed position) that encodes the direction. The same tile character must always produce an identical pixel block, and different tile characters must produce different blocks.
- build_assets.py defines, as plain Python literals at module level: CELL; BOARDS = {"board1": [row strings], ...} with 5-6 boards, each 7-10 columns by 7-10 rows, at least half of them square; EXAMPLE = [row strings], a small NON-square board (for example 3x6 or 4x7) that contains every tile character used on any board, with ONE allowed exception when you apply strategy H2: one confusable tile type may be left out of the example if RULES.md documents its exact appearance (base RGB triple, marker RGB triple, and marker size and position in pixels); the pipeline checks those numbers against the rendered pixels. It saves board images as "boardN.png" in its working directory (/app/fixtures) and the example as "../docs/example.png" (create that directory if needed). Use one-character tile codes ('.', '#', 'S', 'G', and so on).
- docs/RULES.md documents the rules, the CELL size, the drawing conventions above, and a PARTIAL legend: the colors of floor, wall, start, and goal only. It says that the remaining tile types appear in docs/example.png, that docs/example.txt shows the same board in text form, and states in words what each remaining character means (for example '>' is a conveyor pushing right, '+' is a charge pad) WITHOUT giving its color or marker. The pipeline writes docs/example.txt from EXAMPLE; do not write it yourself.
- The board text must not appear anywhere the agent can read: only in build_assets.py (deleted after the image build) and in the hidden tests.

BOARD QUALITY
- Every rule matters: for each plausible simplified reading of the rules (see NAIVE_VARIANTS below), at least one board's minimal solutions change. Spread the rules across boards so that most boards exercise at least two of them.
- Each board is solvable; its minimum number of moves is 7-14; it has 2-20 minimal sequences (all must be listed); its minimal solutions exercise the interacting rules, so an agent that ignores or simplifies a rule gets a different answer; the start and goal are not adjacent. Think through the minimal solutions while designing each board.
- Open floor creates hundreds of equally short paths (a 7-move route through open floor can have 30+ orderings). Use walls and special tiles to channel movement into corridors so only a few routes are minimal; boards with more than 40 minimal sequences are rejected.

ANSWER FILE AND TESTS
- instruction.md: short and natural. Say: solve every board in /app/fixtures under the rules in /app/docs/RULES.md; write /app/answer.txt with one line per board, in board order: "boardN: <minimum number of moves> <all minimal move sequences, sorted ascending, separated by single spaces>"; the boards are only available as images; show one example line. (The pipeline appends a time-box paragraph.)
- Do NOT write answer.txt or BUG blocks: the pipeline creates the placeholder answer file and the per-board starter gaps, and fills the reference answers from the values your tests compute.
- tests/test_outputs.py: use the names BOARDS and EXAMPLE WITHOUT defining them (the pipeline injects the literals from build_assets.py at the top of the module). Implement the rules as three module-level functions: initial_state(rows) -> a hashable state (position plus every piece of changing state); step(state, move, rows) -> the next state, or None if the move is illegal exactly as RULES.md says; is_goal(state, rows) -> True when the puzzle is solved. Build solve(rows) -> (min_moves, sorted list of all minimal move strings) on them with a BFS that keeps EVERY predecessor reaching a state at the same depth (never drop an equal-length path to an already-seen state, or minimal sequences go missing); the pipeline cross-checks solve() against an exhaustive enumeration built on initial_state/step/is_goal. Then define:
    NAIVE_VARIANTS = {"short-name": step_function, ...}: 3-5 alternative step functions with the same signature as step(), each implementing ONE plausible but wrong simplified reading of the rules that a careless solver would write (ignore one exception; apply an interaction in the obvious order; treat a rare tile like a common one). The pipeline rejects the task unless each variant changes the minimal solutions of at least one board.
    def expected_line(name): returns f"{name}: {k} " + " ".join(seqs)
    def _answer_lines(): the non-blank, stripped lines of /app/answer.txt (assert the file exists)
    def test_line_count(): assert len(_answer_lines()) == len(BOARDS)
  and one test per board, exactly like:
    def test_board1():
        exp = expected_line("board1")
        record_expected("board1", exp)  # predefined helper: never define it; call it BEFORE asserting
        lines = [l for l in _answer_lines() if l.split(":")[0].strip() == "board1"]
        assert len(lines) == 1 and " ".join(lines[0].split()) == exp
  Tests must not decode images and must not import anything from /app.

The task must be original and different from the already-generated tasks listed by the user (different mechanic, different domain nouns).

OUTPUT FORMAT. Reply ONLY with these blocks, in this order. Write file contents verbatim; each block header is a line of its own.

=== META ===
{"slug": "short-kebab-case-descriptive-name", "summary": "one sentence describing the task", "strategies": ["H1", "..."]}
=== FILE instruction.md ===
<verbatim markdown>
=== FILE README.md ===
<short plain-language overview for humans; do not reveal answers or tile encodings>
=== FILE app/docs/RULES.md ===
<rules, drawing conventions, partial legend>
=== FILE fixtures/build_assets.py ===
<CELL, BOARDS, EXAMPLE literals and the renderer>
=== FILE tests/test_outputs.py ===
<verbatim pytest module>
=== END ===
